title: The joy of learning
hookLine: the Psalms call the Torah sweeter than honey (Psalm 19:11)
tomorrow: Noa's studied with Eli every night. does the Torah ever say stop?

lines: A WIN THE SIZE OF A TEXT.
A LINE THAT COMES OUT WHOLE.
cards: A win small enough to fit in a text message. The chord you couldn't play, and then could. The recipe that finally tastes like your grandmother's.
A line you've stumbled on all week, coming out whole. That rush has a flavor, and a Psalm names it. It says God's teachings are sweeter than honey.
And an old custom took the Psalm at its word, and put real honey on the page.

teach.h: MORE THAN GOLD. SWEETER THAN HONEY.
teach.b: Psalm nineteen praises God's teaching, and then says of it, in the JPS translation: "More to be desired are they than gold, yea, than much fine gold; sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb." Gold is something you keep.
Honey is something you taste, right now, on your tongue. The Psalm picks both.

Tradition tells of a custom, kept in some communities, for a small child's first day of learning: the letters of the aleph-bet, written out and touched with honey, so the first taste of Torah would be sweet.
The Talmud has its own picture.

teach.h: A FIG TREE: ALWAYS ONE MORE.
teach.b: In the tractate Eruvin, the words of Torah are compared to a fig tree. Every time you search a fig tree, you find another fig. Every time you go back to a text, you find another taste.
So joy isn't the reward you get after the hard part is over.

teach.h: JOY IS PART OF THE LEARNING.
teach.b: It's part of the learning itself: the line that finally clicks, the question that opens instead of closing, the evening a cousin dances in the kitchen because he got a verse right.
Something to tell a friend tonight: in some communities, a child's first lesson came with honey on the letters.

how: Some Jewish communities mark a young child's first day of Torah study with honey on the letters of the aleph-bet, and Psalm 19 is part of the Shabbat morning psalms in many prayer books.

games.q: what does “the joy of learning” mean?
o: the sweetness found inside study itself
the relief you feel once the studying is over
a reward a teacher gives for a finished lesson

games.q: the taste of learning — tap the pairs.
p: more than gold, sweeter than honey
honey on the letters, in some communities
part of the study, not after it

s: Torah study is meant to be serious work, not something you enjoy
Psalm 19 calls God's teaching sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.
the honey-on-the-letters custom is commanded in the Torah itself
it's a later custom kept in some communities, taking the Psalm at its word.
the Talmud compares words of Torah to a fig tree
in Eruvin: every time you search it, you find another fig.

games.q: your friend just aced the hardest piece in her music exam and texts "lol it's just relief it's over." what would the fig tree say?
o: it's more than relief: the joy is part of the learning, and there's more to find.
she's right: the joy of learning is just the hard part ending.
she should stay humble and not enjoy it too much.
games.why: in Eruvin, words of Torah are a fig tree: every search finds another fig. the joy comes back each time you return.

practice: If you have something sweet nearby, a raisin, a spoon of honey, a piece of fruit, take one small taste. While it's still on your tongue, say one line you love, slowly, from these lessons or from anywhere.
Let the two sit together until the sweetness fades.

wordCard.voice: The joy of learning: the sweetness the Psalm finds in God's teaching, more than gold, more than honey. It belongs inside the study, not after it.

orig.note: Hebrew: honey. Psalm 19:11 calls God's teaching sweeter than d'vash.

carryVoice: Your line: sweeter than honey. A fig tree always has one more fig. Talk tomorrow.
